l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L24: Digital applications and extended-answer technique.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Describe the features of gaming applications, simulations and mobile apps. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Digital applications are programs that help people learn, train, stay in touch, work, bank and shop. Gaming applications use rules, levels, points, leaderboards and immediate feedback to motivate players, and online multiplayer lets people play and talk together in real time. Simulations use a computer model, built from data and mathematical rules, to copy how a real object or situation behaves, so people can test designs or practise dangerous tasks safely. Virtual reality takes this further by placing the user inside a 3D world through a headset.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Mobile phone apps are always with the user and use features such as notifications, GPS and the camera to support learning, communication and work on the move. Online banking, online training and e-commerce have changed how we manage money, gain skills and buy goods. Each brings clear benefits, such as 24/7 access and convenience, but also drawbacks, such as fraud risk, the need for internet access and digital skills, and less face-to-face contact. In the exam you must be able to describe the features and uses of the first three and evaluate the impact of the last three on both users and organisations.
Right. What else do we need to know?

Games suit training because they are built in levels: each level brings a new challenge and you cannot skip ahead, so skills are built step by step. Immediate feedback shows the learner what went well and what to try next, and role play lets them make decisions and reflect on the results without real consequences. Leaderboards and badges, often called gamification when they are added to non-game tasks, encourage people to keep improving. Simulations are used where real practice would be dangerous, expensive or rare.
Got it. Keep going.

A trainee pilot can face engine failure or a thunderstorm in a flight simulator, with every action recorded for feedback, and no fuel is used and no aircraft is taken out of service. Surgeons can rehearse an operation on a 3D virtual patient made from scan data. Mobile apps let teachers share video, audio and e-books, let pupils reach their work through the cloud at home and school, let managers message groups of staff, and let schools tell parents about events. Good apps load quickly, keep personal data secure, can be personalised and are kept up to date by their developers.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Online banking lets customers check balances, view statements, pay bills, transfer money and set up standing orders and direct debits at any time, even from abroad, and Faster Payments moves money almost instantly. However, customers need a device, an internet connection and the skills to use it, so some older or less confident people are excluded. Fraud is a real worry: phishing emails and fake texts try to steal login details. Some customers miss face-to-face help.
Okay. Keep going.

For banks, online services cut costs because fewer branches and staff are needed, and e-statements save paper and postage, but banks must protect huge amounts of personal data with complex, constantly updated security and must employ specialist staff. Online training lets employees learn at their own pace and at a convenient time, saves travel, lets staff in different places train at once and records progress automatically. Multimedia and VR simulations make it engaging and realistic. On the other hand, support may be limited to FAQs or email, learners can feel isolated, it needs self-motivation, deadlines are hard to manage and a poor connection can stop learning altogether.
Go on.

E-commerce means buying and selling goods and services over the internet. For customers it is convenient: they can shop at any time without travelling, which especially helps people with disabilities, parents of young children and those living far from town centres. They can read reviews, compare prices, choose from a far wider range than a local shop stocks and pre-order popular items. For businesses, there is no need for expensive high-street premises or checkout staff, so savings can be passed on as lower prices, and a website can reach customers worldwide. The drawbacks are also real.
Right. Keep going.

Customers cannot see or try goods before buying, so items may not match the photos and must be posted back. They wait for delivery and often pay extra for it, and fake websites may be set up to steal card details. Secure payment services and checking for HTTPS reduce this risk. In the UK, the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 usually give online shoppers 14 days after receiving goods to cancel the order. High-street shops may close as more people shop online, affecting town centres and jobs.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
E-commerce?
The buying and selling of goods and services over the internet.
Online banking?
Using a bank's secure website or app to manage an account, for example viewing statements, paying bills and transferring money.
Online training?
Learning delivered over the internet, often with multimedia and automatic progress tracking, that learners can complete at their own pace.
Gaming application?
An electronic game played on a console, computer or mobile device, often online with other players.
Gamification?
Adding game features such as points, badges and leaderboards to a non-game activity to increase motivation.
Simulation?
A computer model, built from data and mathematical rules, that copies how a real object or situation behaves so it can be tested or practised safely.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

This topic is almost always tested through 6-mark extended questions that also assess quality of written communication: advantages of online training, disadvantages of online shopping for customers and disadvantages of online banking to the customer. Shorter questions have asked for drawbacks of online learning, risks of gaming and matching key terms such as e-commerce. Answers are marked in levels: roughly Level 1 (1-2 marks) for a few basic points, Level 2 (3-4) for some developed points and Level 3 (5-6) for several well-developed, accurate points in an organised answer using specialist terms. Read the question carefully: if it asks about the customer, points about the bank or business earn nothing, and if it asks for disadvantages, advantages are not credited. Develop every point with a reason or consequence. Words such as 'faster', 'easier' or 'cheaper' on their own are not credited, so explain what is faster and why it matters. Spell key terms correctly and write in paragraphs.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. What is the name for buying and selling goods and services over the internet? Is it A, E-commerce; B, E-safety; C, Batch processing; D, Cloud gaming?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is A: E-commerce. E-commerce is short for electronic commerce: trading online.
